title: Primitive types
context: What are Java's primitive types, and how do they behave in arithmetic and as values?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): Java basics questions (1 of 3)
source.note: Question and topic from this JavaGuide article. The answer is an original English write-up; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: Java has eight primitives: `byte` (8 bits), `short` (16), `int` (32), `long` (64), `float` (32, IEEE 754), `double` (64), `char` (16-bit unsigned UTF-16 unit) and `boolean`. They are stored by value and are not objects. Integer overflow wraps silently, so `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` is negative. Floating-point types cannot store most decimal fractions exactly, so use `BigDecimal` for money. Integer division truncates toward zero.

points.title: Overflow wraps
points.why: int arithmetic overflows without an exception. Use Math.addExact or long when a bound matters.

points.title: Floating point is inexact
points.why: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in double. Money needs BigDecimal.

points.title: Primitives are not objects
points.why: Primitives have no methods and are not null. Wrapper types like Integer are needed for generics and null.
